turns.doctor_question: Hello, please have a seat. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, I suppose I’m here because things have been... complicated at work lately. I’m a secondary school teacher, you see, and I’ve been teaching for quite a long time, so I know how things are supposed to run. But recently, over the last few weeks—or maybe it’s been a couple of months now, time just sort of blurs when you're grading papers every night—I've been noticing these... peculiarities. 

It started with the morning announcements. You know, the usual things over the intercom, reminding students about club meetings or cafeteria rules. But the phrasing... the specific words the principal uses. It's like there's a second layer of meaning there, specifically directed at me. And then there are the staff emails. We get dozens of them, of course, about curriculum updates or staff meetings, but I can't shake the feeling—no, the absolute certainty, really—that some of them are coded messages. Like, they’re written in a way that seems innocent on the surface, but if you look closely at the syntax or the timing of when they hit my inbox, it's clear they're about my teaching methods, or my personal life, or... well, just about me. 

I’ve tried talking to a few of my colleagues about it. Sarah, the history teacher next door, she’s very sweet, and she’s sat down with me and gently pointed out that the emails are on the all-staff mailing list. She even showed me her inbox to prove she got the exact same message at the exact same time. And I see what she’s showing me, I really do. I look at her screen, and I see the email. But it doesn't change this overwhelming, heavy feeling in my chest that the message was still meant for me, hidden right there in plain sight. It’s exhausting, honestly, trying to decipher it all while still trying to teach thirty teenagers about literature, and I just... I don't know how to turn it off.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, unshakeable belief that general staff emails and school announcements contain coded messages specifically directed at them, which persists even when presented with contradictory evidence by a colleague.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from noticing these coded messages, have you been hearing any voices or sounds that other people don't seem to hear?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, it’s funny you should ask that, because... yes, actually. But it’s not—I mean, it’s not all the time, and it’s certainly not like a booming voice from the heavens or anything dramatic like you might see on television. It usually happens when things are very, very still. 

You know how a secondary school is, it’s absolute chaos from the moment the first bell rings until the final dismissal. The noise is just a constant, overwhelming hum of lockers slamming and teenagers shouting and chairs scraping against linoleum. But after 3:30, when the students have all rushed out to catch their buses or go to sports practice, and my classroom finally empties out... there’s this profound, heavy silence. And it’s in those moments, or later on when I’m completely alone in the quiet of my own house, just sitting at the kitchen island making a cup of Earl Grey tea or organizing my lesson plans, that I hear it. 

It’s a woman’s voice. She just... says my name. Or sometimes she’ll make a very brief, short comment about exactly what I’m doing right in that exact moment, like, "She's turning the page," or "Putting the pen down." And doctor, it is so incredibly clear. It’s not a mumble or a stray thought in my head—it sounds exactly like someone is standing right over my left shoulder. It’s so distinct and conversational that I actually answer her out loud. I’ll say, "Yes, I'm right here," or "Just a moment, I'm almost finished," and I'll turn around in my chair, fully expecting to see Sarah from next door or maybe one of the custodial staff coming in to empty the wastebaskets, and... there's absolutely no one there. 

I'll even walk out into the hallway to check, thinking maybe someone called out from the corridor and the sound just carried, but the hallway is always completely empty. The overhead lights are half off, the floors are just shining, and I'm entirely alone. It really makes my heart race when that happens, because I just don't understand how sound can travel like that, or if it's just the strange acoustics of the old school building playing tricks on me. But then, like I said, it happens at my house too, and my house is a much newer build, so the acoustics wouldn't be the same at all, which just leaves me trying to figure out who could possibly be speaking to me when all the doors are locked...

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly describes hearing a clear woman's voice saying her name or commenting on her actions when she is completely alone, which she responds to out loud before realizing no one is there.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back to when you first started noticing the coded messages and hearing the voice, has this been happening continuously for more than a month?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, if I really sit down and trace it all back... yes, it’s definitely been more than a month. I’d say it’s been about four months now. I remember because it started right around the time the autumn term began, just after the mid-term break in October. 

I was sitting at my desk, grading a stack of essays on *Macbeth*—which is always a heavy read, as you can imagine, teenagers get so dramatic about Shakespeare—and that was the first time I really noticed the phrasing in the principal's email about the new attendance policy. And then the voice, the woman’s voice... that started creeping in right around the same time, maybe a week or two later, when the days started getting shorter and the school would empty out so quickly in the afternoons. 

So yes, it’s been about four solid months of this. Four months of analyzing every staff memo and turning around in my chair to answer a woman who isn’t there. It feels like much longer, to be honest, because it’s just so exhausting to carry all of this every single day, but on the calendar, it’s been right around four months. I kept hoping it would just sort of fade away over the Christmas holidays when I had a break from the school environment, but it followed me right into the new year, into my own kitchen, just like I was saying before...

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes analyzing staff memos and emails for hidden phrasing, confirming the presence of delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly mentions hearing and answering a woman's voice when no one is there, confirming auditory hallucinations.
